items.q: We've already tried a lot. What's different here?
items.a:
With us, 20 to 40% of the people who attend the masterclass go on to join the training. That comes down to preparation. We put a lot of work into it, because the impact only starts once people take part.

We agree the times with managers in advance, so the training fits into the working week. Your people get to know the programme first, live or in their own time. And we provide the texts, so the invitation comes from your own organisation.

items.q: Doesn't this put the problem on the employee?
items.a: No. You tackle the workload itself through policy: tasks, planning, extra hands in busy weeks. That's still needed. This training comes alongside it. It gives people practical tools for the moments when it still peaks, because those moments won't go away.

items.q: Does everyone have to take part?
items.a:
No, taking part is voluntary. Your people get to know the programme first, live in a masterclass or in their own time. Then everyone decides for themselves.

Our advice: have the invitation come from someone in your own management, saying why you're doing this. People join when they can tell their manager is behind it.

items.q: Is this only for people with stress complaints?
items.a: No, it's for everyone. People who think they're doing fine often notice during the training how much tension they've been carrying without realising. It isn't help for people who are already off sick. It's training to stop it getting that far.

items.q: How does this fit into a full working week?
items.a:
The programme takes one hour a week for six weeks, plus fifteen minutes of practice a day. We fix the times in advance with your managers. And we don't start in the busiest period of your year.

Online and on site both work, and you can choose per group. Research shows online sessions work just as well as in-person ones.

items.q: What about privacy?
items.a:
Every participant gets their own impact report. Individual answers never go to the employer. You only see the results for the group as a whole.

We sign a data processing agreement with you, and the data is stored on servers in Europe.

items.q: How do we pay for this?
items.a: You pay per participant. You get a quote in advance, so you can reserve the budget.

items.q: Can we start small?
items.a: Yes. Start with one school, department or team where the pressure is high and management is on board. If it works, you roll it out further, with the results of the first group to show.

items.q: How do you make sure the learning environment is safe and comfortable?
items.a: The training has weekly group workshops with up to 15 participants. People practise in a safe and comfortable way by responding to concrete questions, without having to share personal stories. So everyone feels at ease and can fully practise with attention.

items.q: 15 minutes of practice a day, how does that work?
items.a: Participants get a workbook at the start with a piece of theory and short exercises for each week. They also receive audio recordings of the exercises. Some exercises can be done during daily routines like brushing your teeth, showering or doing the dishes. So it doesn't cost any extra time. Other exercises take about 12 minutes. For those, you need a quiet spot.

items.q: What are the exercises?
items.a: All exercises are aimed at training attention. The goal is for participants to work and live with more focus and awareness. That's why the exercises are directly applicable in daily life, for example while brushing teeth, eating or walking. Each week also includes a 12-minute exercise.

items.q: What is the foundation of Innerleaps?
items.a: Innerleaps' awareness trainings build on evidence-based programmes such as MBSR, MBCT and WorkplaceMT. The foundation rests on 12 scientific studies, including multiple meta-analyses and randomized controlled trials. The evidence is strong enough that the U.S. military has incorporated attention training into its official doctrine (U.S. Army Field Manual 7-22), and organisations like Google, Apple, Microsoft, Nestlé and Unilever have implemented similar programmes.

items.q: What does an Innerleaps programme deliver for our employees?
items.a:
Research into this kind of training finds less stress, fewer burnout symptoms, more resilience and better sleep. Take stress: compare someone who did the training with someone who didn't, and in 65 to 72% of cases the trained person has less stress.

The risk of long-term absence drops by 70% (from 54.4% to 16.4%). And the drop in stress lasts: studies that checked back three months to a year later still found measurably less stress.

items.q: What is sustainable employability?
items.a: Sustainable employability means employees can keep working in a healthy, motivated and productive way throughout their career. In practice it usually breaks down at the same point: long-term work stress. A quarter of all absenteeism in the Netherlands is stress related. Innerleaps tackles that cause. Employees learn to spot and regulate tension early, so dropout is prevented rather than repaired.

items.q: How do you reduce absenteeism without it staying at symptom relief?
items.a: Reducing absenteeism only works structurally if you step in before people drop out. A quarter of all absenteeism in the Netherlands is stress related. Our training teaches employees to recognise stress signals early, so absenteeism does not just fall but stays low.

items.q: How quickly do we see results?
items.a: Participants notice a difference after the first workshops, and that effect builds up over the six weeks. Straight after the 6-week training, 70% report experiencing less stress. It also lasts: research shows stress stays lower for months after the training.

items.q: Why are the masterclass and the training online?
items.a: Research shows that online is just as effective as in person. Because it's just as effective, we choose the option that costs participants the least time. No travel time, just from home or the office.

items.q: Why would my employer want to cover the training?
items.a: Stress costs employers a huge amount of money. Both in sick leave and in lower performance. Employers are happy to help you improve this. We hand you a brochure that makes it easy for your employer to understand and approve.

items.q: 15 minutes of practice a day. How does that work?
items.a: When you start you get a workbook from us. It contains a piece of theory and short exercises for each week. You also receive audio recordings of the exercises. Some exercises you do during daily activities like brushing your teeth, showering or doing the dishes. So no extra time. Other exercises take about 12 minutes. For those, you need a quiet spot.

items.q: What are the exercises?
items.a: Participants do their "brain push-ups" in two ways. In the planned training you do a 12-minute audio exercise each day where you focus your attention on your breathing or your body. Sounds easy? Your mind doesn't think so. Within seconds you're thinking about your to-do's or that meeting. Every moment you bring your focus back is the push-up that strengthens your control centre. You also train in your daily life by bringing conscious attention to everyday activities. During your morning coffee, on your way to work or before you go into an important meeting. It costs no extra time and you become more productive in what you do.

items.q: What if I miss a week?
items.a: If you miss a session you can call the trainer to still get all the information. The workbook also contains everything you need. For the best result it's important not to miss more than one session.

items.a:

Productivity goes up too. The effect is smaller, but it is the result the studies agree on most.

The risk of long-term absence drops by 70% (from 54.4% to 16.4%). And the drop in stress lasts: studies that checked back three months to a year later still found measurably less stress.

items.q: How does Innerleaps improve my performance?
items.a:
Innerleaps improves your performance by optimising working memory, the mental "workbench" where thinking, deciding and acting happen. This works through three mechanisms:

First, relevant information is selected faster and irrelevant information is suppressed better. Your concentration increases, distraction decreases. Research shows up to 24% improvement on attention tasks (Jha et al., 2021).

Second, stress and pressure normally occupy a large share of working memory. When that pressure decreases, capacity is freed up for the task itself.

Third, working memory becomes more efficient: better results with less neural effort (Bailey et al., 2020). You perform sharper and have energy left at the end of the day.

Third, working memory becomes more efficient: better results with less neural effort (Bailey et al., 2020). Employees perform sharper and have energy left at the end of the day.
